Thin Keys, Full Values:
Reducing KV Cache via Low-Dimensional Attention Selection

Hengshuai Yao Affiliation: Sapient Intelligence Affiliation: Department of Computing Science, University of Alberta Email: hengshu1@ualberta.ca    Guan Wang Affiliation: Sapient Intelligence Email: one@sapient.inc
Abstract

Standard transformer attention uses identical dimensionality for queries, keys, and values (dq=dk=dv=dmodeld_{q}=d_{k}=d_{v}=d_{\text{model}}). Our insight is that these components serve fundamentally different roles, and this symmetry is unnecessary. Queries and keys produce scalar attention weights (selection), while values carry rich semantic representations (value transfer). We argue that selection is an inherently lower-dimensional operation than value transfer, requiring only 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) dimensions to distinguish among NN relevant patterns. We validate this hypothesis across seven experiments: (1) positional selection tasks requiring just 1 dimension per head, (2) content-based retrieval requiring ∼log2⁡N\sim\!\log_{2}N dimensions, (3–4) WikiText-2 and WikiText-103 language modeling where dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4 incurs only 4.3% perplexity increase while reducing QK parameters by 75%, (5) post-training SVD compression of GPT-2, revealing keys to be far more compressible than queries, with lightweight QK fine-tuning recovering nearly all quality loss, (6) a 125M-parameter LLaMA model confirming identical degradation ratios across architectures, and (7) Mistral-7B (7.2B parameters), where SVD compression followed by QK fine-tuning achieves 75% key cache savings at just 2.0% residual quality cost. For existing models, SVD compression followed by QK fine-tuning (3 epochs on a small fraction of pretraining data) achieves 75% key cache savings at <<2% residual quality cost. For a 7B-parameter model serving 128K context, asymmetric attention saves 25 GB of KV cache per user, enabling approximately 60% more concurrent users on the same GPU.

1 Introduction

The self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017) computes:

Attention​(Q,K,V)=softmax​(Q​K⊤dk)​V\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V (1)

where Q=X​WQQ=XW_{Q}, K=X​WKK=XW_{K}, and V=X​WVV=XW_{V} are linear projections of the input sequence X∈ℝn×dmodelX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\text{model}}}. In virtually all modern transformer architectures—GPT (Radford et al., 2018), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023)—the projection dimensionality is identical: dq=dk=dv=dmodeld_{q}=d_{k}=d_{v}=d_{\text{model}}.

This symmetry is a design convention, not a necessity. Attention performs two functionally distinct operations:

  1. 1.

    Selection (Q​K⊤QK^{\top}): Determines which tokens are relevant to each query position. The output is a matrix of scalar attention weights—regardless of the dimensionality of QQ and KK, the product Q​K⊤∈ℝn×nQK^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} contains only scalar similarity scores.

  2. 2.

    Value transfer (attn⋅V\text{attn}\cdot V): Extracts and aggregates information from the selected tokens. The output must preserve the full representational capacity of the model, carrying semantic, syntactic, and positional information forward through layers.

These operations have fundamentally different complexity requirements. Selection is a ranking problem: given a query, assign higher scores to relevant tokens and lower scores to irrelevant ones. By the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma (Johnson and Lindenstrauss, 1984), distinguishing among NN items in a dot-product space requires only 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) dimensions. Value transfer, by contrast, must preserve the full informational content of the model’s representations.

We propose asymmetric attention, in which queries and keys project to a lower-dimensional space dselect≪dmodeld_{\text{select}}\ll d_{\text{model}} while values retain the full model dimensionality:

Q\displaystyle Q =X​WQ,WQ∈ℝdmodel×dselect\displaystyle=XW_{Q},\quad W_{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{select}}} (2)
K\displaystyle K =X​WK,WK∈ℝdmodel×dselect\displaystyle=XW_{K},\quad W_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{select}}} (3)
V\displaystyle V =X​WV,WV∈ℝdmodel×dmodel\displaystyle=XW_{V},\quad W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{model}}} (4)

The attention computation proceeds unchanged—Q​K⊤/dselectQK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{\text{select}}} produces scalar weights that are applied to VV. No architectural modifications are required beyond changing projection dimensions.

This simple modification yields three practical benefits:

  • •

    Parameter reduction: WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} shrink by a factor of dmodel/dselectd_{\text{model}}/d_{\text{select}}, reducing attention parameters by up to 75% when dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4.

  • •

    KV cache reduction: During autoregressive inference, the key cache stores K∈ℝn×dselectK\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\text{select}}} instead of ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\text{model}}}, directly reducing the dominant memory bottleneck in long-context serving. For a 7B-parameter model at 128K context, this saves 25 GB of KV cache per user, enabling ∼\sim60% more concurrent users on the same hardware.

  • •

    Attention compute reduction: The Q​K⊤QK^{\top} product requires 𝒪⁡(n2⋅dselect)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot d_{\text{select}}) operations instead of 𝒪⁡(n2⋅dmodel)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot d_{\text{model}}).

We validate asymmetric attention through a progression of increasingly complex tasks, providing both theoretical motivation and empirical confirmation that selection operates in a lower-dimensional space than value transfer. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    A theoretical and empirical analysis showing that attention selection is inherently low-dimensional. We demonstrate that queries and keys require only 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) dimensions, validated across positional selection (1 dim/head), content-based retrieval (log2⁡N\log_{2}N dims), and language modeling (dmodel/4d_{\text{model}}/4 incurs only 4.3% PPL cost), with consistent results across three architectures (vanilla transformer, LLaMA, and Mistral with GQA) and scales from 10M to 7B parameters.

  2. 2.

    Asymmetric attention: a simple, drop-in modification that decouples QK and V dimensionality. On WikiText-103, dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4 reduces QK parameters by 75% at 4.3% perplexity cost. Post-training SVD of pretrained GPT-2 reveals keys to be far more compressible than queries, and lightweight QK fine-tuning (3 epochs on <<1% of pretraining data) recovers nearly all quality loss, reducing the residual gap to <<2%.

  3. 3.

    Significant KV cache savings for LLM inference. The key cache shrinks proportionally with dselectd_{\text{select}}, reducing total KV cache by 37.5% when dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4. We provide three deployment paths—training from scratch, SVD + QK fine-tuning, and zero-cost SVD—and show composability with KV cache quantization for up to 16×\times combined compression. For a 7B-parameter model at 128K context, this saves 25 GB per user.

2 Method

2.1 Asymmetric Attention

In multi-head attention with hh heads, standard transformers set dhead=dmodel/hd_{\text{head}}=d_{\text{model}}/h for all of QQ, KK, and VV. We decouple this by introducing dselectd_{\text{select}}, the total dimensionality for queries and keys:

dheadQ​K=dselecth,dheadV=dmodelhd_{\text{head}}^{QK}=\frac{d_{\text{select}}}{h},\qquad d_{\text{head}}^{V}=\frac{d_{\text{model}}}{h} (5)

For each head ii, the attention computation is:

Qi\displaystyle Q_{i} =X​WQ(i),WQ(i)∈ℝdmodel×dheadQ​K\displaystyle=XW_{Q}^{(i)},\quad W_{Q}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{head}}^{QK}} (6)
Ki\displaystyle K_{i} =X​WK(i),WK(i)∈ℝdmodel×dheadQ​K\displaystyle=XW_{K}^{(i)},\quad W_{K}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{head}}^{QK}} (7)
Vi\displaystyle V_{i} =X​WV(i),WV(i)∈ℝdmodel×dheadV\displaystyle=XW_{V}^{(i)},\quad W_{V}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{head}}^{V}} (8)
headi\displaystyle\text{head}_{i} =softmax​(Qi​Ki⊤dheadQ​K)​Vi\displaystyle=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q_{i}K_{i}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}^{QK}}}\right)V_{i} (9)

Critically, no projection is needed between the attention weight computation and the value aggregation: the attention weights softmax​(Qi​Ki⊤/dheadQ​K)∈ℝn×n\text{softmax}(Q_{i}K_{i}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}^{QK}})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} are scalars regardless of dheadQ​Kd_{\text{head}}^{QK}, and they multiply ViV_{i} of any dimensionality.

When dselect=dmodeld_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}, this reduces to standard multi-head attention. When dselect<dmodeld_{\text{select}}<d_{\text{model}}, selection operates in a compressed space.

2.2 Theoretical Motivation

We argue that selection requires 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) dimensions where NN is the number of distinct patterns the attention mechanism must distinguish among.

Selection as a ranking problem.

The attention weight αi​j∝exp⁡(qi⊤​kj/d)\alpha_{ij}\propto\exp(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}) assigns a scalar relevance score to each key kjk_{j} given query qiq_{i}. For correct selection, the mechanism must ensure that relevant keys score higher than irrelevant ones. This is a ranking problem in the dot-product space of QQ and KK.

Dimensionality for ranking.

By the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, NN points in high-dimensional space can be embedded into 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) dimensions while approximately preserving pairwise distances. For attention, this means 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) dimensions suffice to maintain the relative ordering of dot-product similarities among NN candidate keys.

What determines NN?

In language modeling, NN is not the vocabulary size but the effective number of distinct selection patterns—the number of meaningfully different categories the attention mechanism must distinguish for routing purposes. These include syntactic roles (subject, verb, object), semantic clusters (topic-related tokens), and recency patterns. Empirically, this effective NN appears to be in the hundreds to low thousands, much smaller than vocabulary size, suggesting dselect≈10d_{\text{select}}\approx 10–2020 dimensions per head should suffice.

Value transfer requires full dimensionality.

Unlike selection, value transfer must preserve the complete representational content of tokens—their semantic identity, syntactic role, positional information, and contextual meaning. This information is distributed across all dmodeld_{\text{model}} dimensions of the model’s representations, and compressing VV would discard information that downstream layers require.

2.3 Post-Training Compression via Factored Keys

Asymmetric attention can also be retrofitted to pretrained models via low-rank approximation of the key projection. Given a pretrained weight matrix WK∈ℝdmodel×dmodelW_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{model}}}, we compute its truncated SVD:

WK≈Ur​Σr​Vr⊤,Ur∈ℝdmodel×r,Σr∈ℝr×r,Vr∈ℝdmodel×rW_{K}\approx U_{r}\Sigma_{r}V_{r}^{\top},\quad U_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times r},\quad\Sigma_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},\quad V_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times r} (10)

where r=dselectr=d_{\text{select}} is the target rank. This yields two factors: A=Ur​Σr∈ℝdmodel×rA=U_{r}\Sigma_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times r} and B=Vr⊤∈ℝr×dmodelB=V_{r}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{model}}}, such that WK≈A​BW_{K}\approx AB.

The critical observation is that AA and BB can be separated and assigned to different roles. In standard attention, the key for token jj is kj=xj​WK∈ℝdmodelk_{j}=x_{j}W_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}, producing a dmodeld_{\text{model}}-dimensional vector that must be cached. With the factored form:

kj=xj​WK≈xj​A​B=(xj​A)⏟∈ℝr​Bk_{j}=x_{j}W_{K}\approx x_{j}AB=\underbrace{(x_{j}A)}_{\in\mathbb{R}^{r}}B (11)

We define AA as the new key projection: WKnew=A∈ℝdmodel×rW_{K}^{\text{new}}=A\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times r}. This produces rr-dimensional keys kj′=xj​A∈ℝrk_{j}^{\prime}=x_{j}A\in\mathbb{R}^{r}—these are what we store in the cache, at a fraction of the original size.

To preserve attention scores, BB is absorbed into the query projection. The original attention score between query position ii and key position jj is:

qi​kj⊤\displaystyle q_{i}k_{j}^{\top} =(xi​WQ)​(xj​WK)⊤≈(xi​WQ)​(xj​A​B)⊤\displaystyle=(x_{i}W_{Q})(x_{j}W_{K})^{\top}\approx(x_{i}W_{Q})(x_{j}AB)^{\top}
=(xi​WQ​B⊤)​(xj​A)⊤=qi′​kj′⁣⊤\displaystyle=(x_{i}W_{Q}B^{\top})(x_{j}A)^{\top}=q_{i}^{\prime}\,k_{j}^{\prime\top} (12)

where qi′=xi​WQ​B⊤∈ℝrq_{i}^{\prime}=x_{i}W_{Q}B^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r} and kj′=xj​A∈ℝrk_{j}^{\prime}=x_{j}A\in\mathbb{R}^{r}. The new query projection is WQnew=WQ​B⊤∈ℝdmodel×rW_{Q}^{\text{new}}=W_{Q}B^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times r}—a simple matrix multiplication applied once, adding no runtime cost since queries are computed fresh each step and never cached.

The result is mathematically equivalent to training with dselect=rd_{\text{select}}=r from the start: queries and keys are rr-dimensional, values remain at dmodeld_{\text{model}}, and the key cache stores only rr dimensions per token. No retraining is required; the entire conversion is a one-time factorization of WKW_{K} per layer.

2.4 KV Cache Implications

During autoregressive generation, models cache KK and VV for all previous tokens to avoid recomputation. For a model with LL layers serving context length nn:

Standard KV cache =2⋅n⋅dmodel⋅L⋅b​ bytes\displaystyle=2\cdot n\cdot d_{\text{model}}\cdot L\cdot b\text{ bytes} (13)
Asymmetric KV cache =n⋅(dselect+dmodel)⋅L⋅b​ bytes\displaystyle=n\cdot(d_{\text{select}}+d_{\text{model}})\cdot L\cdot b\text{ bytes} (14)

where bb is the bytes per parameter (2 for fp16). With dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4, the K cache shrinks by 75%, yielding a total KV cache reduction of 37.5%. At scale—128K context, 32 layers, dmodel=4096d_{\text{model}}=4096, 100 concurrent users—this translates to approximately 2.5 TB of memory savings.

3 Experiments

We validate asymmetric attention through seven experiments of increasing complexity: two controlled algorithmic tasks that isolate positional and content-based selection, two language modeling benchmarks at 10M-parameter scale, post-training SVD compression with fine-tuning recovery on GPT-2, a 125M-parameter LLaMA model confirming architecture generality, and SVD + fine-tuning at 7B scale on Mistral-7B.

Experiments 1–4 use a standard transformer decoder with pre-norm layer normalization, GELU activations in the feed-forward network, and learned positional embeddings. Experiment 6 uses the LLaMA architecture (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE). In all cases, the only variable across configurations is dselectd_{\text{select}}.

3.1 Experiment 1: Positional Selection (Copy-Back Task)

Setup.

We design a task where each token must copy the token from K=8K=8 positions earlier: yt=xt−Ky_{t}=x_{t-K}. The source position is fixed regardless of token content, isolating purely positional selection. Sequences of length 64 are generated with random tokens from a vocabulary of 16. The model uses dmodel=64d_{\text{model}}=64, 4 heads, 2 layers.

Results.

Table 1 shows that even dselect=4d_{\text{select}}=4 (1 dimension per head) achieves 100% accuracy, though convergence is slightly slower. This confirms that positional selection—learning to attend to a fixed offset—requires minimal dimensionality.

3.2 Experiment 2: Content-Based Selection (Key-Value Retrieval)

Setup.

We construct sequences of 8 random key-value pairs from a vocabulary of 16 tokens, followed by a query key. The model must output the value associated with the queried key. Positions are randomized each batch, so positional information is useless; the model must match content. Architecture: dmodel=64d_{\text{model}}=64, 4 heads, 4 layers.

Results.

Table 2 reveals a sharp transition between dselect=4d_{\text{select}}=4 and dselect=8d_{\text{select}}=8. With 1 dimension per head, keys map to scalars and cannot be reliably separated via dot product, achieving only 65.2% accuracy. With 2 dimensions per head, keys can point in distinct angular directions, enabling perfect matching. The 𝒪⁡(log2⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}N) prediction gives a lower bound: 16 keys require log2⁡(16)=4\log_{2}(16)=4 dimensions total, but the model needs a small constant factor above this minimum to learn reliable separation via gradient descent. In practice, dselect≈2​log2​Nd_{\text{select}}\approx 2\log_{2}N appears sufficient.

3.3 Experiment 3: WikiText-2 Language Modeling

Setup.

We train causal language models on WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017) ( 2M training tokens) with dmodel=256d_{\text{model}}=256, 8 heads, 6 layers, dff=1024d_{\text{ff}}=1024, sweeping dselect∈{8,16,32,64,128,256}d_{\text{select}}\in\{8,16,32,64,128,256\}. Word-level tokenization with vocabulary size ∼\sim29K (min_freq=2\text{min\_freq}=2). Training uses AdamW with cosine learning rate schedule for 30 epochs.

Results.

Table 3 shows that dselect=64d_{\text{select}}=64 (dmodel/4d_{\text{model}}/4) achieves a test perplexity of 122.24, essentially identical to the baseline of 122.22. Even dselect=32d_{\text{select}}=32 loses only 1.3%. Notably, dselect=128d_{\text{select}}=128 outperforms the baseline (120.76 vs 122.22), likely because reducing QK capacity acts as a regularizer in this heavily overfitting regime (train PPL 37 vs validation PPL 127).

Connecting to the 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) prediction.

The vocabulary contains ∼\sim29K words, yet dselect=64d_{\text{select}}=64 (8 dimensions per head) suffices. This implies that the effective number of selection patterns NN is far smaller than the vocabulary size. Intuitively, attention does not need to distinguish every individual word from every other—it needs to distinguish categories of tokens relevant to different attention patterns: syntactic roles (subject vs. object vs. modifier), semantic clusters (topic-related words), positional patterns (recent vs. distant tokens), and punctuation or structural cues. The number of such categories is in the hundreds, not the tens of thousands. With 8 heads each operating in 8 dimensions, the model can represent ∼28=256\sim\!2^{8}=256 distinguishable patterns per head, which appears to be sufficient for the selection demands of language modeling. This is consistent with the observation that attention heads tend to specialize into a modest number of interpretable roles (positional, syntactic, rare-word) rather than implementing vocabulary-sized lookup tables.

3.4 Experiment 4: WikiText-103 Language Modeling

Setup.

To eliminate overfitting as a confound, we repeat the experiment on WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017) ( 100M training tokens) with the same architecture. Word-level tokenization with min_freq=200\text{min\_freq}=200 yields a vocabulary of ∼\sim22K. We train for 10 epochs with batch size 64 and 2000 warmup steps.

Results.

Table 4 shows the clean comparison. With 50×\times more training data, the model is capacity-limited (train PPL ≈\approx val PPL), eliminating the regularization confound. Here dselect=128d_{\text{select}}=128 (dmodel/2d_{\text{model}}/2) incurs only a 2.1% perplexity increase with 50% QK savings, and dselect=64d_{\text{select}}=64 (dmodel/4d_{\text{model}}/4) incurs 4.3% for 75% savings—larger than on WikiText-2, confirming that the WikiText-2 result was partly masked by overfitting. Nevertheless, the tradeoffs remain compelling: the relationship between dselectd_{\text{select}} and perplexity is smooth and monotonic, allowing practitioners to choose their operating point on a clear Pareto frontier.

3.5 Experiment 5: Post-Training Compression of GPT-2

Setup.

We apply SVD compression to projections in pretrained GPT-2 (124M parameters, dmodel=768d_{\text{model}}=768, 12 heads, 12 layers) without any retraining. Given a weight matrix W∈ℝdmodel×dmodelW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{model}}}, we compute its truncated SVD W≈A​BW\approx AB where A∈ℝdmodel×rA\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times r} and B∈ℝr×dmodelB\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{model}}}, reconstruct the approximation, and evaluate perplexity on WikiText-2. We test three modes: compressing both WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K}, KK-only, and QQ-only.

Results.

Table 5 reveals a striking asymmetry. Compressing both WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} is catastrophic—at rank 192, errors in QQ and KK compound through the softmax, producing a cross-term ΔQ​ΔK⊤\Delta_{Q}\Delta_{K}^{\top} that destroys attention patterns. However, compressing KK alone is far more forgiving: rank 384 (dmodel/2d_{\text{model}}/2) incurs only 2.0% degradation.

Notably, KK is substantially more compressible than QQ at every rank. At rank 192, KK-only degrades by 26% while QQ-only degrades by 181%. This suggests that keys encode relatively structured, low-rank token properties (“what I am”), while queries encode more complex contextual needs (“what I need”) that vary more across positions and layers.

Deployment via factored keys.

The SVD factorization provides a direct path to KV cache reduction. Given WK≈A​BW_{K}\approx AB where A∈ℝdmodel×rA\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times r} and B∈ℝr×dmodelB\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{model}}}, we can split the computation:

K′\displaystyle K^{\prime} =X​A∈ℝn×r\displaystyle=XA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} (store in cache — small) (15)
Q′\displaystyle Q^{\prime} =X​WQ​B⊤∈ℝn×r\displaystyle=XW_{Q}B^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} (compute at query time — discarded) (16)

The attention scores are preserved exactly:

Q​K⊤=(X​WQ)​(X​A​B)⊤=(X​WQ​B⊤)​(X​A)⊤=Q′​K′⁣⊤QK^{\top}=(XW_{Q})(XAB)^{\top}=(XW_{Q}B^{\top})(XA)^{\top}=Q^{\prime}K^{\prime\top} (17)

The key cache now stores rr-dimensional vectors instead of dmodeld_{\text{model}}-dimensional ones, while B⊤B^{\top} is absorbed into the query projection at no additional memory cost (since QQ is computed fresh each step and never cached). This means our KK-only PPL measurements directly reflect deployment performance with actual cache savings:

Interpretation.

Post-training SVD of WKW_{K} alone provides a viable, retraining-free path to moderate KV cache savings. However, the achievable compression is limited: KK-only SVD at dmodel/4d_{\text{model}}/4 (rank 192) degrades by 26%, whereas training from scratch with dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4 costs only 4.3% on WikiText-103.

Recovery via QK fine-tuning.

Can fine-tuning recover the SVD quality loss? We compress WKW_{K} via SVD, then fine-tune only the QK projections (∼\sim21M of 124M parameters) on WikiText-103 for 3 epochs over 10M tokens—a small fraction of GPT-2’s original pretraining data. To isolate the effect of compression from general domain adaptation, we include a control: rank 768 (no compression) fine-tuned identically.

The results are striking: fine-tuning QK projections for 3 epochs nearly eliminates the SVD quality loss. At rank 192 (dmodel/4d_{\text{model}}/4), the gap shrinks from +27.6% to just +1.8% relative to the identically fine-tuned control. The SVD provides a good initialization—the top-rr singular vectors capture the most important selection directions—and the QK projections need only learn to route information through fewer dimensions while the rest of the model remains frozen. This establishes a third deployment path: SVD compress + QK fine-tune, achieving 75% key cache savings at <<2% quality cost with minimal compute.

3.6 Experiment 6: Architecture Generalization (LLaMA 125M)

Motivation.

All training experiments so far use 10M-parameter vanilla transformers. A natural concern is whether asymmetric attention generalizes across architectures and scales. We validate on a faithful LLaMA implementation at 125M parameters—12.5×\times larger.

Setup.

We implement a standard LLaMA architecture with RMSNorm, SwiGLU FFN, Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), no bias terms, pre-norm residuals, and tied embeddings (Touvron et al., 2023). The only modification: WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} project to dselectd_{\text{select}} dimensions; WVW_{V} remains dmodeld_{\text{model}}. When dselect=dmodeld_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}, the model is exactly standard LLaMA. Configuration: dmodel=768d_{\text{model}}=768, 12 heads, 12 layers, dff=2048d_{\text{ff}}=2048, ∼\sim101.7M parameters at baseline. Training: WikiText-103 with vocabulary truncated to 22K tokens (min frequency 200), 5 epochs, batch size 64, sequence length 512, cosine schedule with 2000-step warmup.

Results.

The degradation ratios are remarkably consistent across architectures and scales:

dselectd_{\text{select}} 10M Vanilla (Exp. 4) 125M LLaMA (Exp. 6)
dmodel/4d_{\text{model}}/4 +4.3% +4.3%
dmodel/8d_{\text{model}}/8 +7.6% +7.2%

The +4.3% cost at dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4 is identical across architectures despite a 12.5×\times scale difference and completely different design choices (LayerNorm vs RMSNorm, GELU vs SwiGLU, learned positions vs RoPE). At dmodel/8d_{\text{model}}/8, the degradation is also closely matched (+7.6% vs +7.2%). This strongly suggests the QK dimensionality requirement is a fundamental property of the attention mechanism, not an artifact of any particular architecture.

3.7 Experiment 7: SVD + Fine-tuning at Scale (Mistral 7B)

Motivation.

Experiments 5–6 demonstrate SVD compression and architecture generalization at up to 125M parameters. To confirm these findings hold at the scale of modern LLMs, we apply the SVD + QK fine-tuning pipeline to Mistral-7B (7.2B parameters), a widely used open-weight model with Grouped-Query Attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, dmodel=4096d_{\text{model}}=4096, 32 layers).

Setup.

Mistral-7B uses GQA, so the key projection is WK∈ℝ4096×1024W_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{4096\times 1024} (8 KV heads ×\times 128 dims per head), yielding a key dimensionality of 1024. We compress WKW_{K} via SVD to ranks 512, 256, and 128, then fine-tune only the QK projections on WikiText-103 for 3 epochs over 10M tokens (batch size 1, gradient accumulation 8, sequence length 2048, learning rate 5e-5, bf16 precision). A control (rank 1024, no compression) is fine-tuned identically. All runs use a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.

Results.

The SVD + QK fine-tuning pipeline scales to 7B parameters with consistent quality. At rank 256 (75% K cache saved), the residual gap is just +2.0% relative to the control—matching the GPT-2 result (Table 7) almost exactly. At rank 512 (50% K cache saved), the gap is a negligible +0.3%. The before-FT degradation at rank 256 is larger for Mistral-7B (+17.1%) than for GPT-2 (+10.4% at the equivalent dmodel/3d_{\text{model}}/3 rank), reflecting the more complex learned representations of a 7B model, but fine-tuning recovers nearly all of the loss.

These results confirm that the SVD + QK fine-tuning approach is practical at production scale: compressing key projections in a 7B model, then fine-tuning only the QK projections (∼\sim671M of 7.2B parameters, 9.3%) for 3 epochs on 10M tokens, yields 75% key cache savings at ∼\sim2% quality cost.

4 Analysis

4.1 Scaling of Minimum dselectd_{\text{select}}

Our experiments reveal a consistent pattern in the minimum dselectd_{\text{select}} required for different selection tasks:

The empirical results are consistent with the 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) prediction. For language modeling, the effective NN appears to be approximately 256, suggesting that attention selection operates over a few hundred distinct semantic/syntactic categories rather than the full vocabulary space.

4.2 Overfitting Masks the Effect

The WikiText-2 vs WikiText-103 comparison reveals an important methodological point: on small datasets, reducing dselectd_{\text{select}} can appear costless (or even beneficial) because the model is overfitting. The WikiText-2 baseline has a train/val PPL ratio of 3.4×\times, indicating massive overfitting. Removing QK capacity acts as implicit regularization. On WikiText-103, where the model is underfitting (train PPL >> val PPL), the true cost of reduced dselectd_{\text{select}} becomes visible.

This suggests that results reported only on small benchmarks may overstate the losslessness of QK compression, and that large-scale experiments are essential.

4.3 Practical Benefit: KV Cache, Not Parameters

A potential criticism is that QK parameters represent a small fraction of total model parameters (3–12% depending on architecture), so even a 75% reduction yields modest overall savings. We argue that the primary practical benefit is inference-time KV cache reduction, not parameter savings.

During autoregressive generation, the KV cache grows linearly with context length and must be maintained per user. For a representative configuration (dmodel=4096d_{\text{model}}=4096, 32 layers, 128K context, fp16):

These savings compound with the number of concurrent users and context length, making asymmetric attention directly relevant to the economics of LLM serving. Even the conservative SVD path—requiring no retraining—saves 131 GB per user at 1M context, or 13.1 TB across 100 users. Training from scratch with dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4 extends this to 19.6 TB. At 1M context, a single user’s standard KV cache (524 GB) cannot fit on even 6 ×\times 80 GB GPUs; asymmetric attention reduces this to 4–5 GPUs.

5 Related Work

Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention.

Multi-Query Attention (MQA; Shazeer 2019) shares a single key-value head across all query heads, reducing KV cache by a factor of hh. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA; Ainslie et al. 2023) interpolates between MQA and standard attention by grouping heads. These methods reduce the number of KV heads but maintain dk=dheadd_{k}=d_{\text{head}} within each head. Our approach is orthogonal: we reduce the dimensionality per head for keys (and queries) while keeping the number of heads unchanged. The two approaches can be composed.

Low-Rank Attention.

Linformer (Wang et al., 2020) projects keys and values to a lower sequence dimension: [n,d]→[k,d][n,d]\to[k,d], approximating attention with fewer tokens. Our method reduces the feature dimension: [n,d]→[n,dselect][n,d]\to[n,d_{\text{select}}], maintaining exact attention over all tokens. These approaches are orthogonal and address different bottlenecks. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA; Hu et al. 2022) uses low-rank updates for fine-tuning but does not differentiate between QK and V dimensionality.

Efficient Attention.

Flash Attention (Dao et al., 2022) optimizes the memory access patterns of attention computation without changing its mathematical form. Sparse attention methods (Child et al., 2019; Kitaev et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020) reduce the set of key-value pairs attended to. These are complementary to our approach, which reduces the dimensionality of the QK computation itself.

Compression and Pruning.

Weight pruning and knowledge distillation reduce model size globally. Our work identifies a specific, theoretically motivated target for compression: the key projections are functionally simpler and empirically more compressible than query or value projections. We show that training with asymmetric dimensions from scratch is most effective, but that KK-only SVD followed by lightweight QK fine-tuning can recover most of the quality gap for existing models, paralleling findings that structured compression with targeted fine-tuning approaches the quality of training with constraints from scratch (Frankle and Carlin, 2019).

6 Discussion

Limitations.

Our training-from-scratch experiments use models up to 125M parameters, though SVD + fine-tuning is validated at 7B scale (Mistral-7B). The consistent ∼\sim2% residual gap at 75% K cache reduction across GPT-2 (124M) and Mistral-7B (7.2B)—a 58×\times scale difference—provides strong evidence that the approach generalizes. However, training from scratch with asymmetric attention at 7B+ scale remains future work. Additionally, we evaluate only on perplexity; downstream task performance (in-context learning, instruction following, reasoning) may exhibit different sensitivity to QK dimensionality.

Interaction with Flash Attention.

Most Flash Attention implementations assume dk=dvd_{k}=d_{v} for kernel fusion efficiency. Asymmetric attention breaks this assumption, potentially preventing the use of optimized CUDA kernels. This engineering consideration may offset some of the theoretical compute savings. Future work should develop Flash Attention kernels that support asymmetric dimensions.

Composability with KV cache quantization.

Recent work on KV cache quantization (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024) reduces the bits per element in the cache, compressing keys and values from 16-bit to 4-bit or even 2-bit. Notably, these studies consistently find that keys are more sensitive to quantization than values: KIVI requires per-channel quantization for keys versus simpler per-token quantization for values; KVQuant introduces Pre-RoPE key quantization to handle key-specific outliers; and LeanKV explicitly stores keys at higher precision than values, finding that keys have greater impact on attention computations. This finding is particularly interesting in light of our own: we find that keys are more compressible via low-rank approximation than queries (Table 5). These observations are not contradictory—they reveal complementary structural properties of the key cache. Keys have strong low-rank structure (a few dominant directions capture most of the information), but the residual dimensions contain high-magnitude outliers in specific channels that are critical for quantization. In other words, keys are well-suited to dimensionality reduction but poorly suited to precision reduction—the dominant structure compresses well, but the tail requires full precision.

This suggests that our approach—reducing the number of key dimensions rather than their precision—may be a more natural form of key cache compression, attacking exactly the axis where keys are most compressible while avoiding the axis where they are most fragile. Furthermore, the two methods are orthogonal and compose multiplicatively:

Method K cache / token Reduction
Standard (FP16) dmodel×2d_{\text{model}}\times 2 bytes 1×1\times
Quantization only (INT4) dmodel×0.5d_{\text{model}}\times 0.5 bytes 4×4\times
Thin keys only (dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4, FP16) dselect×2d_{\text{select}}\times 2 bytes 4×4\times
Both (INT4 + thin keys) dselect×0.5d_{\text{select}}\times 0.5 bytes 16×16\times

Thin keys first remove the low-rank redundancy, producing a compact representation with fewer outlier-prone dimensions; quantization then compresses the remaining elements more safely. This pipeline could enable substantially longer contexts or larger batch sizes than either method alone, and we believe studying their joint application is a promising direction for future work.

Implications for architecture design.

The standard convention dq=dk=dvd_{q}=d_{k}=d_{v} has persisted since the original transformer. Our results suggest it should be reconsidered. A simple design rule—set dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4 for the QK projections—yields consistent savings across architectures and scales with minimal quality impact.

Practical adoption path.

We identify three complementary deployment strategies, in order of increasing investment. For existing models with no compute budget, KK-only SVD at dmodel/2d_{\text{model}}/2 provides 25% KV cache savings at 2% PPL cost with zero retraining—a factored key representation where B⊤B^{\top} is absorbed into the query projection. For existing models with modest compute, SVD compression to dmodel/4d_{\text{model}}/4 followed by QK-only fine-tuning (3 epochs on a small fraction of pretraining data) achieves 75% key cache savings at ∼\sim2% residual quality cost, validated on both GPT-2 and Mistral-7B (Tables 7 and 9). For future models, setting dselect=dmodel/4d_{\text{select}}=d_{\text{model}}/4 at training time is the recommended approach, analogous to how Grouped-Query Attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) was adopted: GQA was not retrofitted to GPT-3, but incorporated into LLaMA-2 and all subsequent architectures as a one-line configuration change.

7 Conclusion

We have shown that attention selection (QK) and value transfer (V) have fundamentally different dimensionality requirements. Selection operates in 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) dimensions, while value transfer requires the full model dimensionality. This asymmetry, confirmed across algorithmic tasks, language modeling from 10M to 7B parameters, and three architectures (vanilla transformer, LLaMA, and Mistral with GQA), motivates asymmetric attention: a simple modification that reduces QK dimensionality while preserving V dimensionality.

The practical benefit centers on KV cache reduction during inference—the dominant memory bottleneck in long-context LLM serving. SVD compression of key projections followed by lightweight QK fine-tuning achieves 75% key cache savings at ∼\sim2% quality cost, validated on both GPT-2 (124M) and Mistral-7B (7.2B)—a 58×\times scale range. For production serving at 128K context, this frees 25 GB per user, enabling ∼\sim60% more concurrent users on identical hardware.

We provide three deployment paths: (1) training from scratch with thin keys for maximum benefit; (2) SVD compression of existing models followed by lightweight QK fine-tuning, which recovers nearly all quality loss (from +17% to +2.0% on Mistral-7B, from +28% to +1.8% on GPT-2) using a small fraction of original pretraining data; and (3) zero-cost SVD compression at half rank for immediate savings with no retraining. The approach is orthogonal to both GQA (reducing head count) and KV cache quantization (reducing bit width), enabling up to 16×\times combined key cache compression.
